I now come to the suggestions in connection with the bill. The first has to do with the men and women in the fighting forces, also those who have been discharged from the forces, and with pensioners of the last war. There is some reference to these Canadians in section 8 of the bill, a section which provides against duplication in allowances, and also for the reduction or withholding of allowances. The provision is that there may be a reduction or withholding of the allowance payable-
... to any person receiving aid from the government of Canada or any province for the maintenance of a child in respect of whom the allowance is payable under this act, provided that such reduction or withholding shall not be made by reason of a pension under the Pension Act or dependents' allowance payable in respect of a dependent child of a member of the naval, military or air forces of Canada.
Then section 3 of the bill provides that no allowance shall be paid under the measure until July 1, 1945. I point out to the Prime
Minister that these young men who have been serving in our forces, those who have served and have been discharged, and those pensioned from the last war should be paid at once. I can see no reason why they should not receive their allowances, without waiting until July 1, 1945. I realize that in respect of civilians who have not been in the forces it will be necessary to have registration, to set up records and the like. But in all these other cases, those men and women to whom I have referred, the government has full and accurate records including birth certificates for the children, and I can see no reason for the delay.
Further, many of these people are in great need. For instance, the young wife in Vancouver whose husband is overseas now finds it almost impossible to get a home. We hear some talk about the government's building war-time houses for the dependents of men overseas. There is certainly a great need to help soldiers' families in Canada. Provision should be made to let them have their allowances now, without waiting until July 1, 1045.
I was somewhat disturbed by a press dispatch which appeared in the local papers of July 18, and which purported to be the report of an interview with officials in the Prime Minister's office and in the office of the Minister of Finance. What disturbed me most was this reference to the men of the forces:
One of the reasons that payment of the allowances will not start until July of next year is that the government hopes by that time "Canadian soldiers will be home."
That looks as though it is the hope of the government that it will not have to pay these allowances to the dependents, at all. Then the dispatch goes on to say:
The soldier's wife receives the allowance in addition to all other benefits, and if the troops still are overseas next July "she will be very well off financially," said officials.
I hope the government will go right ahead and make these payments now to the dependents of members of the armed forces, to those who have been discharged and to pensioners of the last war.
Another weakness in the act in regard to the men and women of the armed forces is the fact that children of Canadian fighting men living in England receive no allowance. I have not the figures about the number of Canadians who have married overseas, but I believe it is between 20,000 and 25,000.

But if we look at this question in a sensible light, which I am sure all hon. members can do, it cannot be disputed that no one member of this house has a heart which is very much larger or very much smaller than that of any other hon. member, and that no one party or group have more concern for the welfare of the children of Canada than any others. The love of children is one of the strongest and noblest instincts in man or woman. If we keep these facts in mind and cooperate with each other in trying to make this measure a success, I believe we can hope to do what is set out in the resolution with which the bill was introduced, namely:

We all remember the incident in Roman history when two armies about to engage in battle decided to entrust their fate to the strength and valour of an equal number of men, called respectively the Horatii and the Curatii, rather than have the two armies slaughter one another. At this advanced stage of the session that example might well have been followed by the different parties in this house. As far as I am concerned, I would be willing to let the matter stand for our side on the masterful speech delivered, when he introduced the measure, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); the other parties might have selected each a spokesman to present their viewpoint, and after their remarks had been replied to, the debate could have been closed. I would gladly have accepted such a proposal and, I trust, few members would have opposed it; but as things stand at the moment, after the unbridled flow of words we have heard during the past few days, I have fewer scruples as I rise to go on record on such an important measure.

Family Allowances

deflection of payments that will have to come from other provinces to pay that province's heavier share of these subsidies. A proportionately lower revenue provider receiving a proportionately higher subsidy can scarcely make for greater unity at this stage in our national life.
It is alleged that in Ontario a larger number of families come within the income tax paying group and will, therefore, receive no benefit under this measure. I do not see any injustice- there. If these people, as a result of circumstances I shall discuss in a moment, are better off financially and economically, are we to consider it an injustice when some benefit is given others who in the past have not had the same opportunities or enjoyed the same benefits, and who have not attained the same financial security? It has been said that a larger number of Ontario families are in the income tax paying class. Why? Because of super-intellectual and physical gifts? Because of racial superiority? Well, Mr. Speaker, you might believe that to be the case after listening to the hon. member for Parkdale. From his remarks you would almost think the people of this province have some special attributes.
However, if we calmly analyse the situation we see that half the province of Ontario enjoys climatic conditions which make agriculture at least forty per cent more prosperous than in the colder districts of Quebec. But that is not the main reason for the difference. The main reason is the industries which have been established in Ontario; but those industries have not grown out of thin air. They have been built by capital which came from outside this country, from England and the United States. The people of Ontario have benefited; they have found work and a better standard of living. I do not blame them for taking advantage of this outside capital that has been entrusted to their care; I am sufficiently broad-minded to make that statement. We were the vanquished and they were the victors; money came from England and was entrusted to them, and probably I would have done as they did. But no money came to the Franch-Caandians in the province of Quebec; no foreign capital has been entrusted into their care. Where would it come fromt For a hundred years after 1759 no French ships could sail the St. Lawrence; no connections could be maintained with the former mother country. In all justice I must add that when connections were reestablished no money came from France. They sent their money where it would earn a greater profit, instead of sending it to this country then under British control. So that we had to live to ourselves. Whatever

industries we have established; whatever financial and manufacturing firms we have set up, have been created from the toil and economy of our forefathers, and that point should be taken into account when one is considering the economic situation of Quebec as compared with that of the other provinces. There is no question of inferiority; it was simply the chance that some had to obtain foreign capital, a chance they were sufficiently clever to utilize to their own advantage, and on the other hand the fact that the French Canadian population of Quebec did not have the same chance or the same advantage.
Furthermore, even in those large industries, public utilities, railway companies and so on which have been established in the province of Quebec with capital coming from England or the United States, our people are given minor positions and are prevented from advancing. We do not want to broadcast this situation, as some of the isolationists are doing on the platforms of Quebec at the present time, but we have evidence to that effect. I will admit that for some technical positions our people may not have been qualified, because our province has not had the schools in which people may be trained for these positions, but the progress made during the war is proof of my statement that our people can work a.s well as any others; that when they are given a chance they can better their conditions, working well for the country and helping themselves at the same time. We did not have that chance previously because capital was not entrusted to our people in our province to the extent that it was sent into the province of Onatrio, out the situation has changed with the setting up of the many war plants that now operate in the province of Quebec. For some time last year I was with the empire parliamentary association, and for another period of time I sat on the war expenditures committee. In both capacities I had an opportunity to visit shipbuilding and muntiion plants in Montreal; big gun factories and shipbuilding plants in Sorel; shipbuilding plants in Levis and in Lauzon; small arms ammunition factories and shipbuilding plants in Quebec, and the aluminum plant at Arvida. All these plants were manned by people of my own racial group. They are doing well, occupying positions of importance and responsibility, and with their increased salaries they have bettered their conditions in every way. Therefore that myth of the superiority of the worker of another province, because he is of another race, has vanished with the improved opportunities that have come to the people of Quebec since the beginning of the war. Give any Canadian equal opportunity in industry anywhere, and very

Family Allowances
soon there will be no more talk about Quebec having less people in the income tax paying class than any other province. Give them the same opportunities and the same capital Ontario has had, and they will do just as well; there will be no more suggestions that one group is inferior as compared with another.
All right, Mr. Speaker. We are partly responsible for the past, too, in an indirect way; I am one of those quite ready to admit , that fact. For a long time we lived in a shell, as it were; but discussing the history of those conditions and of that period would, I am afraid, take me far beyond the scope of the question now under consideration. We have been late in developing proper standards of education for the masses. Not having outside capital, we have progressed more slowly in the economic and financial fields. We have not been helped by the immigration of people of our own stock, as others have been helped. We have had no outside capital. Being less self-sufficient financially, the public treasury of our province could not devote the money that should have been spent on health services and in the advancement of educational facilities. I admit all that, but great improvements have been made in the past fifty years. The days of road and bridge building have gone; the period of the harnessing of our water powers and the exploitation of our resources has paved the way for the developments that have been observed in Quebec during the last few years, including improvements in health services, compulsory education, the expansion of technical and trade education and other measures the ultimate results of which will greatly benefit the whole population. Therefore, if perchance thfe margin of benefit accruing to one province seems higher in the aggregate than that accruing to another province, it is partly due to the conditions I have described and partly due also to the fact that the average number of children per family is much larger in Quebec than in the other provinces.
Is there anything unjust about this? A country cannot be said to be prosperous when one part of it is not prosperous. The lack of purchasing power of one part of the population reduces the chances of the other part to better its own standards. We are interdependent more than ever. Nations are interdependent; provinces are interdependent; individuals are interdependent. The advocates of immigration say that we need more population to meet our needs. Let us first improve the lot of our own people, and we shall be sufficient unto ourselves.
I do not think the fears of labour that this treasure may adversely affect salaries are substantiated by the facts. Experts on family allowances connected with the French labour unions in France have all been
witnesses to the fact that that has not been the result of the granting of such family allowances in France. We have the evidence of the secretary-general of the C.G.T.-that is the federation of workers in France-who has stated repeatedly that this had not been the effect over there. We believe the same thing will happen here.
Some people have said that this is an impracticable adventure, and that many of the countries, which had it at one time have had to abandon it. It is to be noted that the eight countries in 1940 which paid family allowances were Belgium, Italy, France, Hungary, Chile, New South Wales, New Zealand and Spain. In addition to these, there are quite a number of countries which paid family allowances on a smaller scale. These were not paid by the government, but rather by the industries themselves. Or, if paid by the government, they are paid solely to the civil service. The civil service, the railway workers, and provincial and municipal employees in Holland receive 2-5 per cent of their salary per child per year with a minimum of 50 and a maximum of 200 florin per head per year.
In Switzerland some industries have instituted family allowances for their own employees. Sixty-five thousand families of employees of the federal administration receive an allowance of 120 Swiss francs per child per year.
In Germany certain industries have had it for a long time, especially the mining industry. Civil servants and day labourers employed on public works, bank and insurance employees have also benefited. The allowances in Germany are uniform for each child.
In Poland the civil servants enjoyed family allowances before the war.
In Czechoslovakia the workers in the coal mining industry received family allowances.
In Austria government employees have benefited from family allowances since 1926. In private industries payment of allowances has been in effect since long before that time. This has applied to mining, steel works, printing establishments, and so on.
In Sweden we find something contrary to what has been said in the house. Sweden never had a government-operated plan of family allowances. Therefore it could not have abandoned such a policy, as has been said. But during the last war the cost of living bonus had taken the shape of subsidies proportionate to the importance of the family. When peace came and normal conditions were restored this cost of living bonus disappeared in 1923.
In Great Britain the greatest objection of the independent labour party is to the fact
Family Allowances

that unskilled labour with large families would receive from their salaries and the allowances paid to them more than would skilled labourers who are bachelors. This objection fails to take into account the fact that the expenses of the father of a family are such that allowances will mean more in the way of benefit to his family, but not more net income to himself than the bachelor would receive.
Fathers of numerous children create a reservoir of vital energy. They contribute to the nation future producers and future consumers. They contribute workers to develop the nation's resources, and consumers of the products of its industries. Yet the fathers of large families are called upon to make the greatest sacrifices. With the policy of equal work with equal pay, which I approve as the only just approach to fair compensation for work, a condition arises where there is inequality of social standing; then inequality of opportunity develops. That condition is opposed to efficiency of the work of the fathers of families. If those fathers are working for the same salaries, they have to deprive themselves of everything in order to maintain their children. Family allowances will correct that condition.
Salary is compensation for a definite economic service which adds to the value of a given product. Allowances are a compensation, for the accomplishment of a social duty, the growth of human capital.
Material difficulties facing families, especially those with numerous children, are such that their number is constantly declining. Yet depletion of human capital and the lowering birth rate have been decried by all economists and sociologists as a major reason for the weakening of many European nations.
I stand by the principle of "equal work-equal salary". The basic salary for work should be enough to provide comfort and decent living to an average family. We were told earlier in the debate that of the: workers gainfully employed forty-eight per cent are single, that thirty-nine per cent have no children under sixteen years of age. _ Therefore the eighty-seven per cent of the gainfully employed are the ones with which we should be concerned in fixing the basic rate. The basic pay should be determined upon decent conditions of living for an average family, and family allowances would then give a supplement to those amounts.
It is understood that the present system as proposed by the government is much more equitable than any other system in operation in Europe before the war. Not only one class of the population, but all of it will be placed

on equal terms. When the allowances are paid only to salaried workers it brings about an exodus from rural to urban communities. People want to get the allowances. The contrary will be the effect under the present measure. Families will be kept on the farms and encouraged to carry on tilling the soil, a process which is so necessary. Migration to cities has been the usual procedure in several countries. If we want to stop that, and if we want to keep carrying on in respect of colonization, then here is the measure which will effect that result.
This is a good measure, much better than those which have been in force in Europe, and which I have had occasion to study. I say that because the measure before the house encourages the man, wherever he is, in the work he is doing. It does not bring about an exodus to the cities, as would happen if only the salaried class were to receive the benefits.
It is said that a few will be taxed to protect the others. That statement fails to take into account the fact that families with many dependents are those which are affected to the highest degree by indirect taxation. They are the largest purchasers of quantity-produced goods, which are the key to prosperity of industrial centres. They are the greatest contributors to indirect taxes, through the great number of things they have to buy daily for their families.
Before concluding, may I say that I found it heartening to hear the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) talk about the narrow-mindedness of the observations of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce). I wonder if the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay realizes that the only utterances of that kind made in the house were made by members of the party to which he belonged in 1940, and of which he was organizer in Quebec, at the time of the-last general election. Unfortunately the hon. member is not in his seat at the moment. It is a known fact that at the next federal election, whenever that may be, in Quebec these people will come out disguised as independents. Just now we see the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) on the platform in Quebec, supporting Mr. Duplessis. Yet he will pledge himself that he is quite independent, when the election comes along.
In conclusion, let me say this, to all the critics of this measure. There are those in my province who have made charges and who will try to find fault with some of the details in connection with the application of this principle. When the hunter in the forest kills a giant bull moose, he rejoices at his success; he marvels at the size of the animal, and his pleasure is enhanced by the struggle he

Family Allowances
has had to get it. He does not stoop to see if the animal has fleas in its fur, but that is exactly what these people are doing now, those in my province or elsewhere who criticize details, especially those who are trying to find fault with the scale of payments, or those who claim that some wfll get more than others. These people are simply trying to find fleas, when they should rejoice that they have received a bull moose as a gift.
They would be contributing more to their own people; they would be contributing more to public life if they tried to realize what the bill really means. We have seen prominent opposition members of this house admit that they agree with the principle of the bill, admit that they are for it but with certain reservations. We have seen certain people in my own province, the people who the hon. member for Parkdale says will benefit most by this bill, finding fault with it. Some people say that this is a political measure, yet we have a group now in Quebec trying to fight it because they do not think it is fair. I think this government has found the proper medium to meet the situation and to provide equal opportunities for our young people. Our political critics will be judged on their merits. As I stated earlier in my remarks, I am ready to let the case stand on the masterful speech delivered by the Prime Minister when he introduced the measure and on the foresightedness he has shown in the past for the advancement and betterment of the fate of the nation.
^ Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview): Mr. Speaker, the opposition has taken up very little time in this debate since the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke the other day. It is the duty and function of the opposition to offer constructive criticism. We have heard a lot to-day about the constitutional question. I come from a city which has been one of the leading cities in America in social reforms of all kinds, and I wish to offer some constructive criticism of the bill. Some of our cities have borne the burden and heat of the day without a great deal of help from the federal authorities.
It is the first duty of the federal government to look after the health, wealth, peace and prosperity of its citizens. Because of our complicated constitution we have had overgovernment and over-taxation in this country. One result has been that the burden bears heavily on real estate, on the small business man, the manufacturer and others who are trying to earn an honest living.

Mr. Speaker, a large part of our representation on this side of the chamber is from the province of Ontario, especially the Toronto district, which has had quite a number of these social services for many years past. These social services grew very largely from beginnings in the days before the South African war, in that glorious Victorian era which built up assets for the future, assets which we seem to have squandered in many ways. In those days the people, kept the state; to-day the trend seems to be that the state will have to keep the people.
We have heard a good deal on this side and other sides of the house concerning the constitutional question, but it has little or nothing to do with this programme. A committee of which I used1 to be a member did some very fine work between the two wars, particularly, in the years 1926, 1927 and 1928. During those~ sessions the industrial and international relations committee examined many witnesses, including the deputy minister of justice, who said that under "public debt and property" federal power could vote money for certain social services. The present Attorney General, who is one of Canada's leading counsel, was one of the principal counsel for the government in connection with the Rowell report. The Rowell commission no doubt did good work, but they discovered very little of importance on the constitutional question not known.( It was well known that none of the social services such as technical education, grants for pensions and the like could be dealt with by the high court of parliament at Ottawa except under the first five or six words of the first section of the British North America Act, having to do with "public debt and property." The subject was dealt with by the Supreme Court of Canada when the government made a reference of then existing 1935 legislation to that court; an appeal was had to the privy council, and Lord Macmillan gave a judgment.
For many years between the two wars I have urged in this house that in view of overgovernment in this country and over-taxation, our main problems in this country were constitutional reform, parliamentary reform, cabinet reform, and law reform; and it turned out, in view of the decisions which have been given, that what I said on this matter was correct. Between the years 1930 and 1935, while the Conservative government was in office, our
Family Allowances

leader adopted a socialistic programme. It was copied very largely from the best of many countries. It was patterned according to a recognition of what Canada could afford to pay for, adapted to our local circumstances, and that should be the test of any social system, for the state has no money to provide for all this work except what comes from the taxpayer. I stated in 1927 andi 1928 that the only authority in the British North America Act under which the fedieral government could provide social services was contained in the words " public debt and property." In the result, in 1935 our government was beaten at the polls, and a new government came in. I remember the blazing billboards all over Canada in 1935, with the colours of the magnificent racing stable at Hamilton-gold and black-and the words "End unemployment; vote Liberal." Was unemployment ended? No; but the people voted Liberal; there is no doubt about that. Along came a continuance of the depression and the dole system. I remember that, sitting across the floor on the front government benches was the late Minister of Labour, the Hon. Norman Rogers, who made the statement to me that what I had said about a billion dollars being spent by federal, provincial and municipal authorities on the dole was correct. And what did they get out of it? Nothing.
I remember when alone in this house, seeing two hundred thousand of our youth coming every year, from 1935 to 1937, out of high school, I advocated an apprenticeship system and an advanced social and security policy for the young people of our country. For this proposal I got no support in this house, I am sorry to say, from my hon. friends to the left. It is true that there were hardly any of them in the house at that time, about the only one being the late Mr. Woodsworth. I wanted to see established an apprenticeship system by which these young people would sign up as apprentices for from three to five years and learn one of fifteen trades, and get military and physical clothing, lodging, a per diem allowance and deferred pay. I suggested that this system should extend from three to five years and include military drill and some knowledge of civil aviation, then in its infancy. With such a system we would have produced in three to five years journeymen fit for some twenty to twenty-five skilled callings, comprising the bigger industries of this country, and when the war broke out we would have had 25,000 skilled pilots and air mechanics. But all we got was the dole, and the dole was a complete failure; to a large extent the money was wasted.

Then came 1935, with the reference of legislation to the privy council. In 1937 I again put forward the apprenticeship proposals for ending unemployment and abolishing the dole. The government of the day appointed the Rowell commission, largely as a consequence of a debate on a motion for parliamentary, constitutional, cabinet and law reform. The late Chief Justice Rowell, who had taken a great interest in the work, headed the commission, and a report was made, but they found out very little except what was known before, namely that under "public debt and property" we could make grants for various social purposes. While I am not speaking for others who live in Ontario, I would state my opinion that the final report of the Sirois commission was unjust and unfair to Ontario, the main taxpaying province of this country. The effect of its recommendations would be to make that province a milch cow for the whole of confederation. However, I do not wish to urge that argument; I never did and I never will, because I believe in the pact of confederation and in the spirit of the old Cornish battle cry, "Each for all and all for each." What is for the benefit of one province should be for the benefit of all the provinces. But from the point of view of social services and the reforms proposed, education and so on, it seems to me that report was unfair to a province like Ontario.
Coming now to the question which has been raised by this bill, No. 161, introduced as a government measure by the Prime Minister-(Mr. Mackenzie King), who has followed this sort of work for many years past, I think he should be well acquainted with the glorious record in the social services of the city from which I come because he and his family have had an intimate connection with that city. It has led in social reforms and services of one kind and another. It is one of the finest cities on the continent and has done a great deal in public health to spread social reform benefits to all classes. Some people seem to think that by means of these family allowances and social security generally we are going to abolish poverty. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we have always had the poor with us and we shall always have them. Neither planning nor victory, nor social reforms, as President Roosevelt has said, will ever bring about the millennium. All the parties in this house seem to have been competing in a race to see which of them could do the most along these letfist lines and which will first reach the sepulchre of social security.
I submit that if this bill had been referred to a select committee of the house we would

Family Allowances
have had a far better measure before us now, because such a committee would have studied all the inconsistencies and inequalities inherent in it, removed the duplication of services, and proposed remedies to remove those many difficulties. As matters stand now under it, we are simply going to set up the largest control system of bureaucracy. The government seems to have forgotten all about the public welfare boards that have already been established in all the provinces and in the larger cities in the dominion. Take, for instance, Toronto. In that city we have a large welfare department dealing with all aspects of the social problem affecting the poor, the sick and the suffering. There is a large office open morning, noon and night, Sundays and holidays, twenty-four hours a day. There are district offices to which the poor can apply. There is a division to look after old age pensions, mothers' allowances and so on; there is an accounting division; there is a single men's division as well as a housing division, and we have a placement division. In emergencies there is a large bureau which will give prompt attention providing food and lodging as well as medical services for neonle in need and takine care of evicted families. I may say that there are 600 soldiers to-night facing eviction orders from their houses. I had a question on the order paper in this connection but it has not yet been answered. We have a department of public welfare to look after all these things, but in this proposed bill the government seem to be altogether unaware of that fact. In one branch of that department in the city of Toronto provision is made for men who are convalescing and there are some per diem patients. Provision is also made for those who are ill and others who are partly employed. There is a physician and there are nurses available. Are we to set up a rival organization in competition with such departments throughout the provinces, ignoring what has been done in the matter for social security? Is the government to overlook all that the city of Toronto has accomplished at great expense, one of the senior municipalities in Canada, which, as I have said, is undoubtedly a leader in social services and has been for many years past?
In another branch of the department to which I have referred provision is made for tubercular cases and there is sanatorium treatment for men who require rest and special food. There is an officer in charge of the placement division which I have mentioned, which works in cooperation with the national selective service to find suitable employment
for persons who, by reason of physical disabilities, require public assistance. Everything is done to help people to get a new start, and those who are in receipt of public assistance are brought before the medical board at intervals. The housing division looks after the cases of persons who are faced with eviction orders and endeavours to prevent eviction. Sometimes it is necessary for people to move a little outside the city. Those on unemployment relief are eligible for consideration. There is provision also for hospitalization. There is an officer in charge of old age pensions and there is a means test.
I suggest that there is going to be a means test under this legislation as well, and in connection with similar social legislation that has been passed in this country. If an old man is in need of help he writes to his son or daughter or some other relative in the family, and if he has a little estate, however small it may be, an old house perhaps, he is refused assistance.
This bill should have been referred to a select committee first and later to the law courts, and in my opinion it may yet wind up there. We have heard a great deal to-day from various constitutional authorities in this house, including the hon. member who preceded me. He seems to be an expert on . all technical questions brought up under the constitution, although he has not had much training in social welfare. Under our con-^'i stitution the courts are subservient to the I legislature and the legislature in turn is ( subservient to the will of the people.	-1
What do we find under this bill? I have been looking through the bill and, while I am criticizing it, I would give it somewhat qualified support. I wish to offer some constructive suggestions to improve it to the government. The first payments under the bill will not be made before July 1, 1945. They have been postponed until that date. There will have been an election before then. The people will have to decide in the ballot boxes once for all whether we are to have a totalitarian socialist state, whether we are to have the programme that has been proposed by hon. gentlemen to my left, whether we are to see in this country the socialization of all services, and whether the Canadian people are to be called upon to exchange for those social services all the liberties that have been won for them down through the years, and submit to regimentation along various lines.
In a dispatch to all Canadian papers from ' the external affairs department on July 18, one of the reasons advanced for the postpone-
Family Allowances

ment of the payment of family allowances until July 1, 1945, is that the government hopes that all Canadian soldiers will be home by that time. That is what is reported to have been said by a government spokesman at a press conference. Well, there is no mandate whatsoever from the people to pass a bill of this kind.
Why have we the right to impose $700,000,000 on the already overburdened taxpayers of this country, with the controls, regimentation, artificial' burdens, barriers and restraints of trade that are now placed upon the taxpayers? Real estate in every municipality in Canada is overburdened with federal problems like this. Why should the city of Toronto have to pay millions of dollars and hand out the dole and all that kind of thing for years, when now the federal parliament are bearing the full burden here as this bill promises to do? The government gave only forty per cent for unemployment, after promising to give it all and end it, and saddled forty per cent on the province and twenty per cent on the municipalities. The weakness of this bill is that it sets up a huge bureaucracy control system. There is duplication in it. The bill has the following elaborate definitions:	"Allowance,
child, institution, maintains, minister, parent, registrations," and so on. How many more registrations are we to have? We have had the census; we have had the unemployment report of the Rowell report; we have had the plebiscite and all these things, and now we shall have a new registration system according to the definition of one section of the bill. Then the bill divides the children into four or five classes. One class is to receive S5 per child per month; another class, $6; another class, $7; another class, $8, and so on.
Instead of having this extensive control board and duplication of services, why do they not make those cash grants direct to the municipalities through the provinces instead of spending two or three hundred millions in the way indicated in this bill? I venture to say they could do the work for one-tenth of the cost if the work were given to the welfare organizations that I have suggested here tonight, the municipalities and the provinces. Much economy could be effected in that way, and only the actual needy provided for.
Under section 9, "powers of minister", they are going to set up a vast body of officials who will make rules and regulations of all kinds. Under section 10 they can arrange with the provinces for the carrying out of the operations of the measure. They make the rules and regulations. There is no definite indication that this $200,000,000 will be well spent. Some

get it and some do not. They say that everybody who can qualify under the section will get it.
When you come to the astronomical figures like that $200,000,000, there is less likelihood that it will be well spent. The disposal of that money will no doubt be by the means test. What about the division of powers? They are going to give to those standing bureaucrats and others the responsibility for spending money voted by parliament.
With respect to the extensive social services of the municipality of Toronto that I shall refer to to-night, one of the main ones in our city is a fine medical health department costing millions of dollars in the past twenty-five years. There is a food inspector, nurses' branch, nutrition branch, dental and medical services, a meat inspector, milk inspector, urban electrification and rural electrification, low cost housing, fuel supply, removal of slums, new sewer supply for the large cities and surrounding districts, pure water supply, transportation system that did so much for housing. Gainful employment for all would do more for the benefit of the working classes than anything else in the history of this country in the way of doles and cash allowances. In our city the fine streetcar system, including buses and radials, under the transportation commission transports passengers for one fare that cost five or six fares throughout the city before. Taking over ol the radials there and removing the light, power and transportation franchises in the counties of Peel, York and Ontario into a civic and district transportation system built up the suburbs. All these things have assisted in the building up of small homes. The up-to-date administration of the health department made it one of the finest on the continent. Education has been well looked after. The public schools, separate schools, secondary schools have all been looked after. There was medical and dental inspection in the schools, free textbooks and no fees to pay. Some people were thirty years of age before they ever saw a dentist. Child welfare and nutrition were taken care of. Milk and meals were supplied in the schools. I would say to the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Cassel-man) that the social services she spoke of have been given the people of Toronto for many years past. In 1910 I became a member and chairman of the board of health, and as alderman, controller and mayor I took a large part in the work of the organization of that department in placing Doctor Hastings in charge. He became one of the greatest medical health officers on the continent.
There is no doubt that had this bill gone to a committee one-third would cover the cost

Family Allowances
of it as it will be or less after the coming election, and about one-third of its cost will have to be assessed against the provinces and the municipalities. A means test will no doubt have to be provided as with other social bills I have mentioned. In our high schools and other schools for some years they have had free textbooks, no fees in any of those schools, and the boon of all these things has been to the working classes of this country.
I am driven to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that we have been overlooking the, war altogether. Generals Beveridge and Marsh are the leading generals of this country to-day. We seem to have forgotten the administration of the war altogether, although it is primary and other things secondary. With an election coming on, we seem to have forgotten all about the war and about the young people who are overseas in Italy, Normandy, Flanders and other places. I have .received letters from some of these boys and they have been wondering what is to happen to them when they get home from the war, whether they will have not only to serve through the war and suffer over there but also have to pay for it when they come back sick and disabled.
If the bill that is before us is to be supplementary and complementary to the low existing wage scale it might have some merit. The minimum wage rates are under the absolute control of the provinces, and excellent work has been accomplished in that connection. I am sorry that this particular bill did not go to the provinces, because I know for a fact that in so far as the legal aspect of it is concerned the province of Ontario has been asking, as others have, for a conference on this subject since the first of the year. With regard to the low wages and the war, there is no doubt that although the workers' wages have gone up, the cost of living has gone up with them, notwithstanding the index. In this particular bill S480 is the limit for a family. Where are they going to get a house for that to-day? There are no houses no matter what you pay for them. That is one of the main social problems before us, proper housing and fuel. There is more ill-health caused by bad housing, lack of ventilation, lack of fuel for nine months of the year than anything else, as any medical officer of health can tell you. In this country fuel is needed for nearly nine months of the year. People can do without food for a day, but they cannot do without a house to live in and little fuel with the temperature as it is for nearly nine months of the year.
This war is not being fought for certain plans, profiles and blueprints of socialism. That is not what we are fighting for in this
war. With regard to those various reports, the Beveridge report is not adapted to this country. It is all very well for us to refer to it, but it is not adapted to this country or to the constitution of this country or to the working classes of this country. Many labour unions have opposed family allowances. They think it will weaken their programme on which they have made progress so far, of better wages and gainful employment with the social services I mentioned and security. Many trades unions take this view which I have supported for many years and some are opposed to family allowances. It will be found that the cost of all those control boards under this bill is going to be fabulous and there will be duplication. With all these controls and boards on all these measures the poor will get very little out of it.
One of the finest institutions in Canada for the care of children is the hospital for sick children in Toronto, which was established by the late John Ross Robertson, and which has become a model for the whole continent. That institution is supported by voluntary subscriptions, and a new building is very badly needed. Eighty per cent of the child patients receive free treatment, while most of the remaining twenty per cent pay very little. I see many of these children, the out-patients, going on the street-car to receive their treatment. I am strongly in favour of helping the families, many of whom are suffering at the present time, but I think considerable economies could be effected in connection with these social measures if we were given a more precise outline of how they are to work. At the present time, of course, there is a great scarcity of domestic help in this country; even those who may be ill and have large families to look after cannot get any assistance, and that situation affects the hospitals and all other social services as well.
The other day the Minister of Finance was referring to the housing situation, but little if anything has been done about it. The Prime Minister of Great Britain has proposed to erect 500,000 prefabricated houses there, but our industries are not likely to receive any large orders for materials entering into such houses unless we aid industry, housing and reconstruction. I doubt if we shall get very much out of that Churchill order, owing to the scarcity of labour and material, any more than we received much benefit from the great orders placed in connection with civil aviation before the war commenced. It was said by a great British statesman two years ago that we should exercise a great deal of caution before making far-reaching decisions in time
Family Allowances

of war, because such decisions are apt to be ill-judged since at a time like this no one is perfectly normal.
The present proposal is fashioned more or less after the Beveridge report, which has been the subject of several debates in the British House of Commons, one of which was referred to by. the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) the other night. On February 26, 1943, in this connection Sir John Anderson, lord president of the council, had this to say:
They (the government) had come to one clear and definite conclusion, that whatever might be decided about cash allowances, by far the best and most effective measure within the limit of its possibilities is the fullest development of the various child welfare services which bring the benefits directly to the children.
That statement was confirmed in the British house later on, although different opinions were also expressed. On March 21, 1943, Mr. Churchill had this to say:
We must beware of trying to build a society in which nobody counts for anything except a politician or an official, a society where enterprise gains no reward and thrift no privileges. I say "trying to build" because of all races in the world our people would be the last to consent to be governed by a bureaucracy. Freedom is their life blood.
That has been the creed of the people of Canada for many years past. Now are we going to give up all our liberties and become a totalitarian state? I say we are not; and it is a case of liberty and freedom on one hand versus state control of our lives on the other. We should restore the right to possess private property, since the real happiness is in gainful work and service to one's fellows, and socialization and the totalitarian state are foreign to our soil and our way of living in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) suggest that the constitutional problem does not arise in connection with the 'measure now under consideration. I quite agree with that statement. I am convinced that the parliament of Canada has full power to legislate in respect of family allowances, and that the bill now before us contains nothing which could be considered in any way an invasion of the provincial field of legislation.
In my remarks this evening I intend to deal with the measure on its merits. At the beginning of the session we were invited to consider a social security and human welfare programme which I think was the finest and most progressive programme ever presented to this house. Some may say that the war is no't yet' won, and that legislation having to do with social security and human welfare might very well wait until it is over. But

while the time of victory is not certain, all signs indicate that victory is now in sight. Moreover, social security and a national minimum of human welfare, together with a closer approach to equality of opportunity, are all part of the new order of which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has spoken and which our men in uniform as well as the civilians of this country will expect to find when the war is over. The Prime Minister has said too that unless the new order is already on its way before the end of the war we may look for it in vain.
Part of the government's great programme of social reform is this provision for family allowances, designed to assist, families whose incomes are low. The scheme is comprehensive, as is quite fitting. The bill provides that the allowances will be paid to families irrespective of family income. There is no limit to the number of children in each family for whom provision is made, although the same amount will not necessarily be paid in respect of each child. The allowances must be applied by the parents, or such other person authorized to receive them, for the maintenance, education and advancement of the children. They may be discontinued or paid to some other person if the Minister of National Health and Welfare is satisfied that the children are not receiving the full benefit. Surely there is nothing wrong in that. These payments will be exempt from taxation. They cannot be assigned or given away as security. The allowances will be paid in respect of children of members of the armed forces and will be in addition to dependents' allowances now provided for their families.
I wish now to give briefly some of my reasons for supporting this measure. It will be generally agreed, I think, that whatever will promote the welfare of the Canadian children is for the good of the country. I would submit that one most effective way of promoting the welfare of our children is to increase the incomes of families of low incomes, in which these children are to be found.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
It is one
excellent way to do it. I do not know of any better way, because family allowances will do this, through the increase in the incomes of these low-income families. They will be able to give their children a better deal. They will be able to provide for them better food, better clothing and better housing, and give them better education. All this will mean

Family Allowances
healthier children. The allowances will permit the children to have a much better chance of success in after years, and to have happier lives.
Family requirements vary according to the number of children, and it is of the utmost importance that provision be made to secure a minimum level of maintenance for the children themselves. An increase in wages of the head of a family will not meet that situation. Wages are based on many factors. They are based on the skill of the workman, the type of work in which he is engaged, and on many other conditions.
It is quite obvious, too, that industry, thrift and self-denial are themselves not sufficient to ensure security. Many people, through no fault of their own, but by reason of illness, unemployment . or possibly unlucky investments, find themselves at times in need of assistance. In a household where the head of a family is able to provide for all reasonable requirements, one would expect to find contentment, and a happy environment in which the children might properly be brought up. On the other hand, if the head of that family is unable to make adequate provision for family requirements, the children may grow up in fear, and with a sense of frustration. The formative years of their lives pass quickly, and in after years they may have to overcome a feeling of inferiority.
It is important that the children in their sensitive years should not feel that family allowances are given on compassionate grounds, and that they can know that, the allowances are received by their tarents as of right. The provision in the bill that allowances are to be paid to families irrespective of income should commend itself to every hon. member.
There is a further consideration. Many heads of families in need of allowances are not wage-earners at all. I have in mind the farmers and the fishermen, and I shall have something more to say about these two classes in a moment or two. Before doing so, however, I wish to suggest, at the risk of repetition, that this legislation will help to create employment in Canada after the war. Our fighting men and women, our war workers and children coming of age will expect, and rightly so, that there will be jobs for them to do. We cannot afford to have it otherwise.
The $200,000,000 a year which it is estimated this programme will cost, will remain in Canada ; it will be spent here. That money will be spent on food, clothing and other family necessities, the supplying of which will in turn help our farmers, fishermen, businessmen and manufacturers. Family allowances will increase the purchasing power of the people. If in the process they also assist in bringing about a more even distribution of our national income, so much the better.
There are some who complain about the cost of the programme. But if we are to have this great measure of social reform we must be prepared to pay for it. So that we cannot afford to abandon our efforts to raise the standard of family life for the masses of the people. We are able to say that in proportion to our population we have put forth the greatest war effort of any of the allied countries. Are we to confess that we cannot raise the money necessary to carry out this great social reform? We have been able to find all the money required for the war effort. If we were called upon to-morrow to supply additional tanks and ships we would not throw up our hands, and say that the money was not available.
In this connection I should like to read a passage from a book written by the Right Hon. Winston Churchill in 1921. This is the book entitled "Aftermath." In the second chapter, speaking about the organization and the machinery at the disposal of the British government on Armistice day, he said this:
There was very little in the productive sphere they could not at this time actually do. A requisition for instance for half a million houses would not have seemed more difficult to comply with than those we were already in process of executing for a hundred thousand aeroplanes, or twenty thousand guns, or the medium artillery of the American army, or two million tons of projectiles. But a new set of, conditions began to rule from eleven o'clock onwards. The money-cost, which had never been considered by us to be a factor capable of limiting a supply of the armies, asserted a claim to priority from the moment the fighting stopped.-
I suggest it all sums up to this, that if family allowances will ensure a national minimum of welfare for our children we should go forward with our programme, and not abandon it because of monetary consideration.
I would congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government upon the courage and vision they have shown in introducing this measure, and in taking steps to see that it is put into effect without any delay. I would submit that the programme of family allowances is inherently sound and in the national interest. I should like, however, this evening to consider it for a few minutes more from a provincial point of view. I hold in my hand a very fine book entitled "The Economic Effects of the War on the Maritime Provinces of Canada," by Professor B. S. Kierstead. His study was made at the invitation of the institute of public affairs at Dalhousie university. One of the chapters
Family Allowances

in the book deals with fisheries, and was written by Professor Stewart Bates, professor of commerce at Dalhousie university, and now economic adviser to the Department of Fisheries in Ottawa. Professor Bates, after referring to the state of the fishing industry at the outbreak of the war, goes on to say:
The money income derived from catching and processing fish in the shore communities averaged less than $300 per annum per man while that of fishermen in larger centres, like that of Halifax and Lunenburg, although averaging $1,000 on bigger vessels, was still low compared to other trades of comparable skill, risk and hardship.
I have referred to the maritime fishing industry because the fishermen are a class who will benefit greatly by family allowances but whose status would not necessarily be affected by an increase in wage levels. In 1939 there were, in Nova Scotia alone, 17,335 inshore and offshore fishermen. I should mention also our farmers. They are also a class not necessarily benefited by an increase in wage levels but who will be greatly benefited by family allowances.
I should like to refer to the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial relations. This report shows that education and welfare expenditures in Nova Scotia are materially below the per capita average for Canada. In the words of the report, "the province shares with New Brunswick the unhappy distinction of having the longest unfavourable economic history of any Canadian province." The per capita wealth of Nova Scotia and the annual income of Nova Scotians are lower than that of most provinces. At the same time living costs are high. In peace time our provincial revenues were insufficient to do more than take care of our normal requirements. They could not possibly support a programme of family allowances such as is proposed. Other provinces with greater resources and more buoyant revenues might be able to do so.
In Nova Scotia where education and welfare expenditures are below the national per capita average, the establishment of a national minimum level of well-being for children would be of tremendous benefit to our people. There is a tendency these days for provinces and municipalities to bring all their problems to Ottawa for solution. Here is a proposal by Ottawa to take care of one of our most pressing and urgent provincial requirements-an improvement in the standard of life of our young children. I welcome and support the splendid programme of family allowances that is proposed.
Let me add one more word. While only 29-63 per cent of the total population of Canada is under sixteen, slightly more than
[Mr. W. C. Macdonald.1
thirty-one per cent of the total population of Nova Scotia is under that age. These figures are based on those given in a return made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) to a question asked by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), to be found on page 4144 of Hansard of June 26 and on the figures to be found in the official handbook, "Canada, 1944", published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
In conclusion, I would say that when one views this measure from all angles it can be safely said that the family allowance programme will be of great benefit to Nova Scotia, financed as it will be by all the people of Canada.
It is fitting that this bill should be sponsored by our beloved Prime Minister. His whole life has been consecrated to the cause of human welfare. He has given magnificent leadership to his country throughout the war. The people of Canada are happy in the certain knowledge that he will continue to lead them, not only until the end of the war, but also in the task of winning the peace that is sure to come.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a few observations on this bill No.-161, to provide for family allowances. The Atlantic charter and the four freedoms expressed an ideal, and we now have a great opportunity to assist in the progress, achievement and welfare of the common man of our country and his dependents. May I say that I have always favoured some form of family assistance.
As a municipal official I had an experience, which I believe is equalled by few members of the present house, during the great devastation and depression-the greatest since confederation-which prevailed1 in the southern part of the prairie - provinces. As a result of the contact I had with many families I became impressed with the necessity for some assistance along family lines. During the years of the depression this same government headed by the same Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) set up what was known as the Rowell-Sirois commission to study conditions in Canada from coast to coast. They spent a great deal of time in receiving many briefs from leading organizations throughout Canada and they duly made their report to the government, I am sorry to think that the present government have completely ignored that report. They have done worse than that; they have added to the difficulties which that report pointed out, by implementing the recommendations of the social insurance commission of the province of Quebec.

Family Allowances
The report of that commission was referred to this afternoon, by my colleague, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). At page 70 of the 1933 second edition of the report of that commission it recommended family allowances rather than providing the same standard of industrial wages which prevailed in other provinces of the dominion. It is pointed out that with uniform rates of wages Quebec could not compete in industrial output with the other provinces. That is scarcely in keeping with the argument which was advanced just before the dinner recess by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard).
My chief criticism of this bill is that it does not create a standard of wages throughout the dominion. This is lacking in various provinces at this time. We tried to provide for this in our amendment which was ruled out of order, and our appeal from the Speaker's decision was voted down by this government. We thought these allowances should not be paid until there was full collaboration with the various provinces and then only after the federal Minister of Labour was satisfied that there were uniform standards of wages prevailing in the various provinces.
I am satisfied that there are people in many parts of this country who would raise larger families if they were assured of an adequate income. I remember a by-election in my native province of Manitoba last year when one of the socialist members was campaigning and endeavouring to prevail on the sympathies of a large audience in the southern part of my province. They had not been in the northern part of Manitoba. I have considerable respect for this gentleman, but he was reported in the press as pointing out the medieval conditions existing in Flin Flon in northern Manitoba. I happened to be in that town at the time he made his speech and I made it my business to find out the conditions which prevailed at that time. I was amazed to find just what the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting company, a capitalistic enterprise, had done for the people in that centre.
These people had splendid homes with modern conveniences which they were able to obtain at reasonable rentals. There were also recreational, educational, health and other facilities provided by this company. Most of the young parents were raising fine, healthy families. To me it was an outstanding example of what could1 be done in a community. It was not in keeping with the thought expressed by that speaker in that by-election who was trying to arouse feeling against capitalism in this country. To me it was evident what could be done in this
country if we had a proper standard of wages throughout Canada. The nation would benefit greatly as a result of healthier and larger families.	.
Again, it was pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that in 1939 the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Claxton), in a presentation to the Sirois commission, pointed out the unconstitutionality of such a measure as that which is now proposed to this house.
It was also pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who, I think, said he had been elected to parliament in 1935, that the first act of the present Prime Minister and his government after being returned to power in 1935 was to scuttle the reform legislation of the Bennett government, and that on constitutional grounds. I believe that is exactly the situation which prevails with this measure to-day. I listened carefully to the arguments of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) on this subject, and I must confess that they did not impress me. I am still convinced that this measure is unconstitutional. To prove our sincerity in this matter, wre proposed an amendment which we thought would make the scheme more workable and which would enable assistance to apply to these people immediately rather than making them wait until July, 1945.
Moreover, I have spoken about my experience during the great devastation and depression in the prairie provinces during the early thirties.
I have been perusing old volumes of Hansard, and I have found a speech by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) under date of February 24, 1930. It is reported in Hansard of that date at page 38. He asserted that relief problems were a matter for the municipalities; if they could not handle the situation, then it was a matter for the provinces; if they could not handle it, then it *was a matter for the federal government, and in the meantime people should mind their own business. I think that makes my stand perfectly clear and shows why I am supporting this bill. I shall have some questions to ask when we are considering the bill in detail, but at the moment I would refer to one section to which reference was made by my colleague the member for Vancouver South, relating to the dependents of those now in the services. speechtext:
I have no desire to prolong the debate before the house, but I wish to offer a few brief remarks om what I consider to be the most important measure designed for the social and economic welfare of the nation which probably has even been brought before this house. That Canada is a resourceful country is something that has never been denied and is a matter of world^wide knowledge. There is no doubt about it that nature has been very bountiful in her gifts to this great dominion, but a superabundance of resources, diversified as they may be, will not alone achieve greatness for Canada. In order to exploit these resources we must have a healthy, vigorous, intelligent citizenship. The adage that the health of the nation is the wealth of the nation has never been marred by the ages; it is just as terse a truth to-day as it was 100 years ago, and the greatest student of economics will point out that the most valuable asset that a nation possesses is a healthy, vigorous, intelligent population; while on the other hand a puny, unintelligent population is the nation's greatest liability.
This bill is designed to improve our social and economic conditions, but under present conditions it is very difficult to enlist into this great and noble programme of betterment every person who is interested in this admirable forward movement. It is impossible under our present conditions to afford equality of opportunity for all who I know are willing to enter into this erusadte. Our w^ige regulations to-day are not flexible enough to take care of the wide discrepancy between the cost of living and his income for the man with a family in the low wage scale, because his income cannot be supplemented and he is not on an equality in earning, from the point of view of the cost of living, with the bachelor, with the young man with no dependents, or the married man who has no family. I believe there is no other corrective for this discrepancy than this very measure that has been brought down to-day. We say that the allimportant thing is to have a healthy, intelligent nation. Take the father of a family in the low wage category. He has to accept the same income as the young man who has no depend-
Family Allowances

emts. How is that father going to carry on. his domestic obligations and' the charges that fall upon him in supporting his family and educating his children? If we are going to propagate and improve the health of our nation, the greatest requisite of all is proper nutrition of the children when they are in their formative years. This bill makes provision for those who cannot afford to give proper, adequate nutrition to their children.
Let us turn next to the question of education. There are many families who will participate in these allowances who can give adequate and proper nutrition to their children. What happens in those cases? These allowances contribute to the better education of their children. If these families can afford to nourish their children they can set aside this allowance so that it will accumulate into a repository that can be utilized later for the advanced education of their children. Those of us who have had experience in teaching school have often been very sorry when we found young children in the lower grades who demonstrated mental acuteness and gave evidence sometimes of the promise of a worthwhile manhood, and who should have had the advantage of going into advanced education. But what happened when they were through with common school education? They were forced to retire from the field of education, and the result is to-day we have some men who inherently are extremely bright but who have had to retire to the pick-and-shovel class simply because they did not have anything to start them on their way. I myself have known young men who, I believe, if they had had enough money to start in their first collegiate year, would have shown such mental assets that many philanthropists, recognizing their ability., would have carried them right through their collegiate course.
With regard to the health side, those of us who have had the experience of practising medicine, particularly in general practice, have seen hundreds of cases of young men and women who I really think went down to an early death because they did not have the resistance to the disease that laid siege to them on account of the lack of proper nutrition in their formative years. As I said at the beginning, I am absolutely of opinion that there never was a measure brought into this house or any other house of parliament that has the same virtue as this measure with which we are now dealing.
Some mention has been made of the cost. Some raised the objection that we are spending $200,000,000, but we must realize that we are spending almost that amount of money 
every day on a programme of death and destruction, almost as much in one day on a programme of death and destruction as we are to pay under this measure in a whole year, a measure that is intended to bring about in this Canada of ours what we think is the initiation of a new day and a new heaven and a new earth. When we consider the dividends that will be paid1 on this small expenditure of money in the way of better health, less hospitalization, less medical costs, less loss of man-power days, I think every lion, member and every individual in Canada will feel that the expenditure is well justified.
Another objection that is advanced against this measure is that there is some fear that the mothers will not make proper use of this money. Having had some experience with mothers in their homes and with their families, I say that I have every confidence in the mothers. I know the solicitude that they have for their children. These mothers who are so tolerant of the restrictions that have been placed upon them during the stress and strain of war, those mothers who have done so much to contribute to this war effort, can be well trusted with every dollar of this money. They will see that it is put aside and used in behalf of the welfare of their children.
We have listened to some other objections. We have heard the constitutional feature of it advanced to-day. I am not a lawyer and I will not enter into that field', but I have confidence in our chief. I do not think he would bring this measure into the house and make the forecast that he made if he did not feel that it was constitutionally operative. I have listened to men on this side of the house who, I think, are just as good authorities as any on the other side of the house. They were supported by the ablest lawyers of the British empire and I am perfectly satisfied that this measure is constitutionally sound.
Then we heard another complaint that this is a matter of bribe. Do you imagine, Mr. Speaker, that our chieftain who has led this great party for twenty-five years would be silly enough on the eve of an election to bribe children who are in the cradle to-day in order to get their votes at the next election? To my mind that is very silly. I will offer this warning to the people who use that as a hurdle to the advancement of this measure, that it is hopeless to expect that when these children come to voting age, which will be twenty-one years from now, they can count on their support for having offered this objection to this great measure which is designed to help the youth of the land.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) says that this measure of social welfare should

Family Allowances
not be brought in at all. He says that in the city of Toronto they have public welfare institutions which are looking after their children. Well, the city of Toronto does not comprise the whole of Canada, and if those philanthropic institutions in Toronto want to carry on with their philanthropy they can do so, despite the fact that this measure comes into effect, a measure in behalf of the youth of the whole of Canada.
The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) suggested that instead of this measure there should be a uniform standard of wages. Well, that will not help the situation of the man , who has a large family compared with the man who has no domestic obligations of that kind. What this bill is designed to do is to bring about equality of opportunity and the establishment of a uniform wage rate would leave matters exactly where they are to-day. As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this is the most important social welfare measure that has ever been brought into this house or into any other house. Despite the criticisms offered and the hurdles that some hon.' members have cast in its path, I believe it is so good and popular and so full of virtue that there is not a man or a woman who sits in this house that would dare undertake to vote against it.
